deep.reconstruction:
Context. This is a remark on Hilbert's own 'Methode der unabhängigen Integrale' (independence-integral method) in the calculus of variations, here for double integrals. The setting is J(z) = ∫_Ω F(x,y,z,z_x,z_y) dω over a plane domain Ω, with z prescribed on ∂Ω.

(1) The original method, recalled on the page. One looks for slope functions p(x,y,z), q(x,y,z), a 'p,q-field'. One forms
J*(z) = ∫_Ω { F(x,y,z,p,q) + (z_x − p) F_p + (z_y − q) F_q } dω,
where p, q, F, F_p, F_q are evaluated at (x,y,z(x,y)). The demand is that J* depend only on the boundary curve and the boundary values of z, i.e. that it be independent of z inside Ω.

(2) The PDE this leads to (my filling-in; standard). Put A = F − pF_p − qF_q, B = F_p, C = F_q. These are functions of (x,y,z) once the field is fixed, and the integrand becomes A + B z_x + C z_y.
- Its Euler–Lagrange expression is A_z + B_z z_x + C_z z_y − (B_x + B_z z_x) − (C_y + C_z z_y) = A_z − B_x − C_y =: E(x,y,z).
- Independence (a null Lagrangian) therefore means E ≡ 0, i.e. ∂_z(F − pF_p − qF_q) = ∂_x F_p + ∂_y F_q.
- This is the system of partial differential equations ('die partiellen Differentialgleichungen') for the field.

(3) The new remark on this page. Instead of independence, Hilbert asks only that J*(z) > J*(z0) for every z with the same boundary values as the given function z0. The PDEs are then replaced by the corresponding partial differential inequalities.

Making this precise (my reconstruction, not on the page):
- Let B̃(x,y,z) = ∫_c^z B(x,y,ζ) dζ and C̃ = ∫_c^z C dζ, with c a constant.
- Then B z_x + C z_y = div(B̃,C̃)|_{z(x,y)} − ∫_c^z (B_x + C_y) dζ.
- Since z = z0 on ∂Ω, the divergence terms cancel. Hence J*(z) − J*(z0) = ∫_Ω ∫_{z0(x,y)}^{z(x,y)} E(x,y,ζ) dζ dω.
- So a sufficient (and essentially necessary) condition for J* to be minimized by z0 is the sign condition (ζ − z0(x,y))·E(x,y,ζ) ≥ 0. That is, E ≥ 0 above the surface z0 and E ≤ 0 below it, a pair of first-order differential inequalities for p, q.

(4) Why this suffices (implicit; continued on the next page).
- If the field is attached to z0 (p = z0_x, q = z0_y on z = z0), then J*(z0) = J(z0).
- Hence J(z) − J(z0) = ∫ 𝓔(x,y,z; p,q; z_x,z_y) dω + [J*(z) − J*(z0)].
- Here 𝓔 = F(z_x,z_y) − F(p,q) − (z_x−p)F_p − (z_y−q)F_q is the Weierstrass excess function.
- Both terms are ≥ 0 under the Weierstrass condition plus the new inequality, so z0 is a minimum.

(5) The next page concludes that, since the same arguments as before apply, the criterion still only requires solving a boundary-value problem for PDEs. Hilbert summarizes: arrange the p,q-field so that z0 minimizes J*. This is a relaxation of the exact field (calibration) requirement to an inequality (sub-/semi-calibration) requirement.

No explicit computation appears on the page itself; it is a conceptual remark.
errors: No mathematical errors on the page. The claim that the PDEs become 'partial differential inequalities' is stated without derivation. The precise inequality (ζ − z0)·(A_z − B_x − C_y) ≥ 0 is my reconstruction.

The assertion (continued on the next page) that 'the same conclusions' follow, so the criterion needs only a boundary-value problem for PDEs, is left vague and unjustified. Solvability of the inequality system with the field attached to z0 is not addressed.

results.what: Hilbert's independence integral J* for double integrals, and the PDE A_z = B_x + C_y on the slope field (p,q) expressing independence from interior values of z
results.modern_name: Hilbert invariant integral / null Lagrangian / field of extremals (calibration) for multiple integrals
results.usually_credited_to: Hilbert (Paris problems 1900, problem 23; Göttingen lectures; 'Zur Variationsrechnung' 1906). Beltrami (1868) and Weierstrass anticipated the one-dimensional case.

results.what: Relaxing independence of J* to the requirement that the given z0 minimize J*, replacing the field PDEs by partial differential inequalities; combined with the Weierstrass excess function this still gives a sufficient condition
results.modern_name: Sufficient conditions via Hamilton–Jacobi inequalities / subsolution verification theorems (cf. Krotov sufficient conditions, sub-calibrations, Carathéodory-type relaxed fields)
results.usually_credited_to: Inequality-based sufficiency is usually attributed to later work: Carathéodory's 'royal road' (1920s–1930s) in spirit, and Krotov (1960s) and verification theorems in optimal control.

deep.surprise_reason: The independence-integral method is well known as Hilbert's. The remark that the PDE for the field may be relaxed to differential inequalities, keeping a sufficiency criterion, anticipates later inequality-based sufficient conditions (Krotov, Hamilton–Jacobi inequalities, sub-calibrations). It is only a sketched aside without precise formulation, so it is a notable unpublished idea rather than a result.
